dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — it's homecoming day: Benji is expected to be discharged today, with his first pediatrician appointment already booked for tomorrow, and Solon is giving you a beautiful day for it, mostly sunny with a high near 73°. It is also Election Day: Ohio polls are open 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM, the governor's race between Amy Acton and Vivek Ramaswamy and the Senate race between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown are both close, and 66 Cuyahoga County precincts — including some in Solon — have new polling places, so check yours before you go. Overnight the U.S. carried out limited strikes on Iranian missile targets on Qeshm Island while talks remained possible, and the Cavs lost a close one to Oklahoma City, 117-112, despite the game staying tight into the final minute. Tonight, after the ride home and a first evening as a family of four (plus Moose), the results start rolling in after Ohio polls close at 7:30.

Death toll rises to at least 29 after Russian bombs hit a Ukrainian aid centre, with 48 still missing
items.summary:
The number of people confirmed dead after Russian aerial bombs struck a school and shelter used to hand out humanitarian aid in the village of Komyshuvakha has risen to at least 29, according to regional officials in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region. Another 10 people were reported injured, and 48 people were still listed as missing as rescue work continued.

The site was not holding classes. Because the village sits close to the front line, residents gathered there on Mondays to shelter and collect aid packages, which made the timing and the crowd predictable. Ukrainian officials described a first strike as people arrived and a second strike on the shelter area.

The updated toll makes this one of the deadliest single strikes on a civilian aid point in recent months, and it landed just a day after a short local ceasefire arranged for aid and evacuations nearby had expired. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also warned that Kyiv has intelligence Russia may be preparing a larger attack timed around the U.S. vote.

Watch for the toll to change again as rubble is cleared, and for whether the strike affects the U.S.-mediated talks scheduled in Abu Dhabi next week.

items.title: Trump says Iran wants a deal 'more than ever' as Qatar circulates a draft to restart talks
items.summary:
President Donald Trump said in a phone interview that he is in no hurry to decide on resuming military action against Iran, arguing that Tehran wants a negotiated settlement more than it ever has. He said the United States had sharply weakened Iran's finances and could afford to give diplomacy more time.

According to Axios reporting relayed in coverage of the interview, Qatari mediators have prepared a draft built around a three-day sequence of confidence-building steps meant to restart direct U.S.-Iran negotiations. A Qatari mediator travelled to Tehran on Monday, and mediators were waiting for responses from both capitals. Vice President JD Vance separately voiced measured optimism about a settlement.

The diplomacy is unfolding alongside force, not instead of it. U.S. forces struck targets on Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, and reporting says Israel's prime minister has urged Washington to consider renewed strikes after the U.S. midterm elections.

Watch for replies to the Qatari draft in the next few days. A yes from both sides would be the first concrete step toward direct talks; silence or new strikes would point the other way.

items.title: Two helicopters collide while landing near Everest, killing an Indian tourist and injuring others
items.summary:
Two helicopters collided as they prepared to land at Pheriche, in Nepal's Solukhumbu district near Mount Everest, on Tuesday morning. An Indian national, identified by police as 47-year-old Vasanth Kumar Balaramaramadu, was killed, and a New Zealander was injured and rescued, district officials told Reuters.

The aircraft were operated by two private companies, Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty. Fishtail said its helicopter was carrying passengers who had been rescued from the Everest region when it crashed while landing. Local reporting put the collision at about 8:11 a.m. local time, as both aircraft came in to the same landing area.

The crash happened in peak trekking season, when helicopters constantly ferry hikers, climbers and cargo through high, thin air and fast-changing mountain weather. Nepal's difficult terrain and safety record have made aviation accidents a recurring concern there.

Watch for the official investigation into how two aircraft ended up on converging landing paths, and for any temporary restrictions on helicopter operations in the Everest region.

items.title: Bangladesh garment workers protest for a fourth day, with tear gas, factory closures and a new wage board
items.summary:
Garment workers in Bangladesh staged a fourth straight day of wage protests on Tuesday, and police fired tear gas to disperse demonstrators in industrial areas around Dhaka. The unrest disrupted factories and transport links in the country's most important export industry.

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka, about $245, up from the current 12,500 taka, saying inflation has eaten away their pay. Clashes were reported in Ashulia, Gazipur and Mirpur, several factories shut or declared holidays again, and nearly 700 factories had closed a day earlier. The government formed a six-member wage board on November 1 to review pay, but that step has not calmed the protests.

Bangladesh is the world's second-largest apparel exporter after China. The industry employs about 4 million people, supplies brands including H&M, Zara and Gap, and accounts for more than 80% of export earnings, so prolonged closures risk delayed shipments in the peak season for spring and summer orders.

Watch the wage board's timetable. A credible path to a higher minimum could settle the streets; a slow process is likely to keep factories and highways disrupted.

items.title: New Zealand heads into Saturday's election in a dead heat, with a small centrist party holding the balance
items.summary:
New Zealand's final major poll before Saturday's general election puts the ruling National Party at 30% and the opposition Labour Party at 29%, a statistical dead heat in the last days of the campaign. The Greens rose to 16%, while National's coalition partners ACT and NZ First both slipped.

Under New Zealand's mixed-member proportional system, neither bloc can govern alone on these numbers. A right bloc of National, ACT and NZ First falls short, and so does a left bloc of Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori. That leaves the centrist Opportunity Party, polling at 6%, as the likely kingmaker either way.

Coalition governments are normal under this system, but a result this tight could mean days of negotiation after election night before anyone can claim a majority.

Watch Saturday's count and, just as closely, what Opportunity demands in exchange for its support, since its price will shape the next government's programme.

items.title: Houthi forces advance to within about 50 miles of Aden, Yemen's temporary capital
items.summary:
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement has advanced to within roughly 50 miles of Aden, the temporary capital and main stronghold of Yemen's internationally recognised government, according to military sources cited by Reuters and summarised in Tuesday's early briefings.

Aden has been the government's base since the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, years ago, and it hosts the central institutions the recognised government still controls. A Houthi push toward it therefore threatens the government's last major urban foothold in the south.

The advance also matters beyond Yemen. The Houthis sit astride the approaches to the Red Sea and have previously attacked shipping there, so a major shift on the ground can quickly become a shipping and energy story as well.

Watch for a government or coalition response around Aden, and for any new threat to Red Sea shipping lanes in the coming days.

items.title: Midterm voting is under way in all 50 states, with more than 57 million ballots already cast and no results yet
items.summary:
Election Day voting is under way across the United States in the 2026 midterms, with control of the House and Senate on the line. Polls opened as early as 5 a.m. ET in Vermont and rolled open state by state through the morning; Hawaii is the last to open, at noon ET. No results have been reported, and none can be until polls start closing this evening.

More than 57 million ballots were cast before Election Day through early and mail voting, according to University of Florida data cited by CBS News. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are being decided, along with 36 governorships.

Analysts and prediction markets favour Democrats to take the House, while the Senate is rated much less certain. The outcome will set the balance of power in Washington for the final two years of President Trump's second term.

Watch the first poll closings this evening, starting with Virginia at 7 p.m. ET, and expect early totals in most states to reflect early and mail ballots first.

items.title: Justice Department sends 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states, drawing praise and pushback
items.summary:
The Justice Department has deployed about 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states for Tuesday's midterms, which the department calls the largest monitoring effort in its history. Officials say the monitors are there to check compliance with federal voting-rights laws.

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said election integrity is a top priority for the Civil Rights Division. The department published lists of the cities and counties receiving monitors and gave voters a hotline, 800-253-3931, for questions or complaints.

Voting-rights groups, including the NAACP, argue the scale and placement of the deployment could discourage turnout, particularly in minority communities, and some local election officials bristled at the implication their elections need federal watching. A federal judge declined late Monday to bar law-enforcement personnel from serving as monitors, finding the challengers had not shown the plan violated the law on the evidence presented.

Watch how the monitors actually operate today. They are barred from interfering with voting, and any documented incident at a polling place will become a legal and political flashpoint fast.

items.title: Courts spent election eve blocking the administration on ballots, and voting itself has run with few problems so far
items.summary:
By Tuesday morning, Associated Press reporting described voting as having unfolded with relatively few problems, with turnout on pace to exceed the last midterms. That calm followed a busy election eve in the courts, where the administration lost several late fights over ballots and election workers.

Among the rulings, the Supreme Court refused to make California set aside about 20,000 mail ballots from voters the Justice Department claims are noncitizens. Separately, the full 9th Circuit voided a panel decision that had paused an order barring threats to prosecute election workers.

The administration had also insisted no armed federal officials would guard polling places. As of Tuesday morning, the steps some officials had feared, such as immigration agents at voting sites or seizures of voting machines, had not happened, according to the AP.

Watch for post-election litigation anyway. Close House and Senate races are likely to be fought over mail-ballot rules in the days after the count, not just on election night.
items.source: Associated Press via Workers Rights News

items.title: Markets and forecasters lean Democratic for the House, but the Senate is the real coin flip
items.summary:
Going into election night, polls and nonpartisan analysts favour Democrats to win back the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains genuinely uncertain. Prediction markets quoted in market coverage put the Democratic chance of taking the House at roughly 95% and the Senate at roughly 75%, though those odds have moved during the campaign.

That split expectation is why investors and campaigns are watching a small set of Senate races most closely. A Democratic House alone would still give the opposition subpoena power and a veto over the administration's legislative agenda; a Democratic Senate as well would also control confirmations.

For Ohio readers, the Senate question runs directly through the Husted-Brown race, one of the contests that will help decide the chamber.

Watch the eastern Senate races first tonight. If they break clearly one way early, the national Senate picture may resolve faster than expected; if they split, expect a long night.

items.title: Trump says the U.S. will end about $4 billion a year in aid to Israel by the end of the year
items.summary:
President Trump announced that the United States will end roughly $4 billion in annual assistance to Israel by the end of this year, saying in a Fox News interview that Israel is now prosperous enough to fund its own defence. The current U.S.-Israel security assistance agreement provides about $3.8 billion a year through 2028.

The announcement drew sharp criticism inside Israel. Yair Golan, who leads Israel's Democratic Party in the anti-Netanyahu bloc, called it a heavy blow to Israeli security at a time when defence spending and the need to rebuild weapons stocks are at their highest, arguing the cost would fall on Israeli taxpayers.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has previously said he wants to reduce Israel's dependence on American military aid over the coming decade. The timing, however, lands in the middle of a war with Iran and a live debate in Washington about whether to strike Iran again after the midterms.

Watch for a formal administration plan. Ending aid set by an existing agreement would require action that Congress is likely to contest, so the announcement is a starting position, not a done deal.

items.title: Apple beats expectations but warns holiday margins will shrink, and the stock falls about 4%
items.summary:
Apple reported quarterly revenue of about $114.5 billion and net profit of about $30.7 billion, both ahead of Wall Street expectations, in the first earnings report under CEO John Ternus. Investors focused instead on the outlook: Apple warned that rising memory-chip costs will keep pressuring its gross margin in the holiday quarter.

The shares fell roughly 4% in premarket trading on Tuesday. That reaction fits a pattern this earnings season, in which strong headline numbers from big technology companies have still been punished when guidance hints that costs, especially around AI hardware, are rising faster than returns.

Apple had recently passed Nvidia to become the world's most valuable company after Nvidia's multi-session slide, so its stumble carries outsized weight in the indexes.

Watch whether the margin warning spreads. If other hardware makers echo it this week, the story becomes an industry cost problem rather than an Apple problem.

items.title: Palantir posts record revenue and raises its outlook, and traders sell the stock anyway
items.summary:
Palantir reported about $2.3 billion in quarterly revenue and about $1.1 billion in net income, both ahead of expectations, and forecast fourth-quarter revenue of about $2.65 billion, above the analyst consensus. Revenue nearly doubled from a year earlier, a record for the AI and data-analytics company.

The shares still fell sharply, down about 8% in premarket trading at one point. Coverage pointed to investor worries about slowing total contract value growth and softer sequential momentum underneath the headline beat.

Palantir's fall, alongside Apple's slide, shows how demanding the market has become for AI-linked stocks after a huge run. Good results are no longer enough; investors want acceleration, and they are selling anything that merely looks excellent.

Watch the close. A recovery by the bell would suggest bargain-hunting; another leg down would confirm the AI trade is still de-rating.

items.title: Nasdaq-100 is now in a correction, down more than 10% from its high, as AI spending worries bite
items.summary:
The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday more than 10% below its all-time closing high, formally putting the tech-heavy index in correction territory. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.07% on Monday and the S&P 500 slipped 0.51%, while the Dow managed a 0.41% gain.

The driver is a shift in how investors judge the AI build-out. After years of rewarding spending announcements, markets are now asking for evidence that the enormous data-centre and chip outlays are producing commensurate revenue, and several big reports this season have not supplied it.

Futures were mixed on Tuesday morning, with chip stocks rebounding: Nvidia rose about 1.4% after four straight down sessions, and AMD gained ahead of its earnings report after the bell.

Watch AMD tonight and the rest of the week's 145 S&P 500 reports. Earnings, not election headlines, are most likely to decide whether this correction deepens or snaps back.

items.title: Shopify misses on revenue for the first time since 2022, and the stock tanks
items.summary:
Shopify fell sharply on Tuesday after third-quarter revenue and gross merchandise volume came in below Wall Street estimates, the company's first revenue miss since 2022. The company still reported about $462 million in net income, with revenue up more than 30% from a year earlier.

A miss of that kind matters more for Shopify than the size of the shortfall suggests. The stock's valuation rests on a long record of meeting or beating expectations, so even a modest slip resets how much investors are willing to pay for its growth.

The result also lands at the start of the holiday quarter, the period that makes or breaks the year for the merchants who run their stores on Shopify's platform.

Watch management's holiday-quarter guidance and any commentary on consumer spending. That will be read as an early signal for online retail well beyond Shopify itself.

items.title: Job openings rose to 7.52 million, and AMD headlines a packed earnings day
items.summary:
U.S. job openings rose to 7.52 million in September, above expectations of about 7.10 million, in the JOLTS report released ahead of Tuesday's session. Preliminary October survey data also pointed to continued expansion, with a manufacturing reading of 55.5 and services at 54.9 in the figures cited in market coverage.

A labour market that is still generating that many openings complicates the interest-rate picture. The 10-year Treasury yield was around 4.91% on Tuesday, and strong demand for workers gives the Federal Reserve less reason to cut quickly.

On the corporate side, AMD reports after the bell and is the day's most watched result. Its shares have more than doubled this year, and analysts expect revenue of about $13.1 billion; Pfizer, Block, Amgen and Super Micro also report.

Watch AMD's data-centre numbers tonight. In a market punishing AI disappointment, its guidance will move the whole chip sector on Wednesday.

items.title: Illinois voters decide whether Gov. JB Pritzker wins a third term against Darren Bailey
items.summary:
Illinois voters are choosing between Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, seeking a third term, and Republican challenger Darren Bailey, in one of the day's most closely watched governor's races outside the battlegrounds. Polls in Illinois are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Late polling gave Pritzker a wide cushion. An ActiVote poll put him ahead 58.7% to 41.3%, Public Policy Polling had him up 54% to 34%, and an average of the two put the race at roughly 56.5% to 37.5%.

Illinois is also one of the states receiving Justice Department monitors, part of the nationwide deployment of about 1,000 observers. Rain showers were expected across northern Illinois during the afternoon, a minor wild card for late turnout.

Watch the margin, not just the winner. A result near the polling average would confirm Illinois as safely Democratic; a much narrower finish would be one of the night's surprises.

items.title: Pennsylvania votes with federal monitors in four counties and its governor's race in the spotlight
items.summary:
Pennsylvania voters are deciding state and federal races today, with the Justice Department sending monitors to polling places in Philadelphia and in Allegheny, Luzerne and Lehigh counties. State officials have told local offices that federal monitors have no more right of access than members of the public and may not enter restricted areas or inspect equipment.

The state is a genuine battleground for the House, so its congressional results will be among the first serious signals of the night after polls close at 8 p.m. ET.

Turnout operations ran all morning across the state, with campaigns and parties publishing photo coverage from polling places as voting proceeded without major reported disruption.

Watch Pennsylvania's suburban House districts tonight. They have a habit of telling the national story early.

items.title: Texas results will arrive in waves tonight, and the close races may take weeks to make official
items.summary:
Texas polls close at 7 p.m. local time on Tuesday, and the Secretary of State's Election Night Returns system is expected to start populating around 7:30 p.m. Central. The first totals in most counties will reflect early and mail ballots, with Election Day votes following as ballots are transported and counted.

El Paso and Hudspeth counties, on Mountain Time, close an hour later than the rest of the state. Anyone in line at closing time can still vote, which can delay the start of reporting at busy locations.

Election Night numbers are unofficial. Counties must canvass and certify before results are final, and the state canvass must occur between November 21 and December 7, so a very close statewide race may not be formally settled for weeks even if a winner is projected tonight.

Watch the attorney general's race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico, one of the most expensive and closely followed contests in the state.

items.title: In Nashville, early voting nearly tripled the primaries, and the mayor is backing voter-protection volunteers
items.summary:
Tennessee voting is under way with polls closing at 7 p.m. in Nashville, where early voting that began October 14 nearly tripled the turnout of the August primaries. Unofficial results will begin with absentee and early-vote totals shortly after polls close.

Justice Department monitors have been sent to Davidson, Shelby and Knox counties, among the roughly 1,000 deployed nationwide. Nashville Mayor Freddie O'Connell has backed a local initiative meant to guard against election overreach, and volunteer groups are assisting voters at polling sites.

Tennessee voters are also deciding a governor's race, making the state one of 36 choosing a governor today.

Watch Davidson County's turnout against the early-vote surge. If Election Day voting is also heavy, Tennessee participation could end well above recent midterm norms.

items.title: Oklahoma officials say the federal monitor presence there is 'extremely limited' and problem-free so far
items.summary:
Oklahoma County's top election official, Doug Sanderson, said the Justice Department monitors dispatched to the Oklahoma City area have an extremely limited presence, and that he had received no reports of problems linked to the observers by midday.

The county was not told in advance exactly where monitors would go and is being notified as they appear. Monitors are also planned for Tulsa and Muskogee counties. Democratic-led volunteer groups have organised their own watchers, focusing on predominantly Black districts in northeast Oklahoma City, in case voters need assistance.

The Justice Department says it prioritised jurisdictions required to provide language assistance and areas with little previous observation data.

Oklahoma voters are deciding a U.S. Senate race and electing a new governor, and turnout was trending higher than in past years, according to local officials.

items.title: Final Ohio poll puts Acton ahead of Ramaswamy by about 8 points, and Brown ahead of Husted by about 7
items.summary:
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy spent election eve campaigning in Toledo and Cleveland, promising to slash property taxes and electric bills and to crack down on crime, with Vice President JD Vance joining him in Cleveland to stump for both Ramaswamy and Senate candidate Jon Husted.

The latest Atlas Polls survey, however, gives Democrat Amy Acton 51.8% to Ramaswamy's 43.9% in the governor's race, a 7.9-point lead. The same poll puts Democrat Sherrod Brown at 51.4% to Husted's 43.9% in the Senate race, a 7.5-point edge.

Polls close at 7:30 p.m. in Ohio, and early totals will lean heavily on the more than a million Ohioans who voted before today. A polling lead of this size can still narrow sharply if Election Day turnout breaks differently than the poll assumed.

Watch Cuyahoga, Franklin and Hamilton counties when the first batches post tonight. Their early-vote totals will show quickly whether the Atlas numbers were in the right neighbourhood.

items.title: Cleveland voting guide: polls until 7:30, bring photo ID, and check your location before you go
items.summary:
Ohio polling places are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. on Tuesday, and anyone in line at 7:30 can still vote. Voters must bring acceptable photo ID, and several Cuyahoga County polling locations have changed for this election, so checking your assigned location before leaving is essential.

Beyond the governor's and Senate races, Cleveland-area ballots include congressional, state legislative and judicial races, county council contests and local tax issues. Cuyahoga County voters can look up a sample ballot by address through the Board of Elections, or call 216-443-8683 for help.

State Issue 3 is the one statewide question: a proposed constitutional amendment on photo identification for in-person voting, with some of the longest ballot language in the country at about 200 words.

If you still hold a mail ballot, it must reach the board by 7:30 p.m. today to count. Dropping it off in person beats mailing it at this point.

items.title: Federal government denies Cleveland $7.8 million lead-safety grant, citing the city as a risky manager of funds
items.summary:
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development has turned down Cleveland's application for a $7.8 million lead hazard grant, according to Signal Cleveland's reporting, not because the need is in doubt but because a risk review rated the city poorly on how it manages federal housing money overall.

City Council member Kris Harsh called the denial terrible news. Cleveland still has three older HUD lead grants running, but all are winding down: a $9.7 million Glenville grant closing at the end of November, a $2 million healthy homes grant closing next June, and a $5.7 million citywide grant closing next July. No replacement federal money is lined up behind them.

For landlords and homeowners, the practical point is that obligations do not change with the grant. Cleveland's Lead Safe Certificate requirements still apply whether or not federal money is available to help pay for the work.

Watch City Hall's response. An appeal, a corrective plan for HUD, or a locally funded bridge would each tell a different story about how Cleveland intends to keep lead work moving.

items.title: Browns waive running back Audric Estime, the Week 6 touchdown scorer, and leave a roster spot open
items.summary:
The Cleveland Browns waived running back Audric Estime on Tuesday, a little over two weeks after his two-yard touchdown run against Baltimore stood as Cleveland's only touchdown in a win. Estime had split the running back carries evenly with Jaleel McLaughlin in Week 6 when injuries thinned the room.

Cleveland announced no corresponding move, leaving an open roster spot a week before the trade deadline. The simplest explanation is a practice-squad elevation, such as tight end Carsen Ryan, but an open spot at this point on the calendar also leaves room for a trade.

The move comes as the 5-3 Browns try to steady themselves after the 27-6 loss in Pittsburgh, with a winnable game against New Orleans on Sunday.

Watch the spot. What fills it in the next 48 hours will say a lot about whether the front office thinks this roster needs a tweak or a real addition.

items.title: Cavs starter Peyton Watson is out with hamstring tightness, adding to Cleveland's wing injury list
items.summary:
Cavaliers starting wing Peyton Watson missed his first game of the season on Monday night after Cleveland ruled him out about an hour before tipoff against Oklahoma City with right hamstring tightness. Coach Kenny Atkinson had said Watson would test the hamstring pregame before the team made the call.

Rookie Meleek Thomas started in his place alongside James Harden, Donovan Mitchell, Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen in the 117-112 loss. The obvious next option, Jaylon Tyson, was also out with a sprained right ankle, his second straight missed game.

Watson, acquired from Denver in a summer sign-and-trade, had started Cleveland's first six games, averaging 10.8 points, 4 rebounds, 3 assists and 1.8 blocks. Hamstring trouble is a familiar problem for him: he missed 25 of Denver's final 30 regular-season games last season with a right hamstring injury.

Watch his status for Wednesday's rematch in Oklahoma City. Given that history, the Cavs have every reason to be cautious rather than quick.

baby.tip: Homecoming day tip: before you leave the hospital, do the car-seat check while help is still right there — base tight, straps snug at armpit level, and Benji's first ride home in a rear-facing seat in the back. Then tonight, keep it simple: one bag unpacked, feeding log started, and the diaper bag restocked for tomorrow's first pediatrician visit. If anything about feeding, breathing or temperature worries you at home, call the pediatrician or your OB team — that's exactly what they're there for.
baby.fact: Newborns sleep a lot but in short stretches — typically 16 to 17 hours a day, broken into naps of just a few hours at a time, because their tiny stomachs need frequent feeding. Benji's sleep will feel random this first week; short, frequent stretches around the clock are completely normal for a brand-new baby.
baby.fun: Today's tiny mission: the first family photo at home — Mike, Kelly, Benji and Moose in one frame (Moose at a calm, supervised distance for take one). It doesn't need to be perfect; the slightly chaotic version is the one you'll love most in a year.
